---
title: "Multi-year temporal deep learning and open satellite data lower the detectability floor for low-severity spruce beetle mortality in Southcentral Alaska"
date: today
author:
  - name: Seamus Murphy
    orcid: 0000-0002-1792-0351
abstract: |
  Spruce beetle (*Dendroctonus rufipennis*) has killed spruce across
  Southcentral Alaska since about 2016, yet roughly ninety per cent of the
  mortality sits in stands of areal severity below 0.05, beneath the detection
  floor of Landsat change analysis, and the aerial survey record understates
  this dispersed damage. Few studies have asked whether the temporal dimension
  of freely available satellite data reaches below that floor, and none has
  asked it of a spruce beetle outbreak in Alaska with radar, which cloud does
  not stop. This study tests whether temporal deep learning on a monthly
  Sentinel-1 radar series lowers the floor, across 160 stand blocks sampled
  over the Southcentral outbreak region and assigned wholly to eight spatial
  cross-validation folds. Terrain-flattened dual-polarisation backscatter from
  one satellite track, speckle-filtered across the length of the series and
  held at 30 m, supplies monthly sums and differences of the two polarisations
  from June 2017 to the present, with climate variables defined from the
  beetle's biology fitted at the same monthly step, to a temporal convolutional
  network and a Transformer encoder trained on dead-spruce crowns digitised
  from statewide sub-metre image mosaics of 2020 and 2023; comparison of the
  two epochs supplies interval-censored mortality-onset labels and a
  cross-epoch consistency check on the labels themselves. Skill is reported per
  severity stratum under block cross-validation against the published
  shortwave-infrared floor, and evaluated independently against a
  high-resolution severity product whose footprint no training fold touches.
  [Detection skill in the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum: pending.] [Detectability floor
  per method: pending.] [Onset-dating error and the effect of interval
  supervision: pending.] [Contribution of climate variables to detection skill:
  pending.] [Correspondence of the reconstructed 2016 to 2025 outbreak
  progression with the aerial survey record: pending.] The severity strata,
  metrics and decision rules were fixed by pre-registration before outcome data
  were analysed.

# Introduction

Recurrent outbreaks of the spruce beetle, *Dendroctonus rufipennis* (Kirby, 1837), Coleoptera, Curculionidae, Scolytinae, have shaped the spruce forests of Southcentral Alaska for centuries, with outbreak extent linked to summer temperature [@Berg_2006]. From 1990 to 2000 an outbreak killed spruce across 1.19 million ha of Alaskan forest, roughly 40 per cent more area than had been infested in the previous 70 years [@Werner_2006], and a new outbreak under way since about 2016 has spread from the Susitna lowlands toward the Alaska Range [@Zwieback_2024]. Where and when beetle-caused mortality occurs, and at what severity, is foundational to hazard management, to carbon accounting and to understanding how a warming climate reshapes boreal disturbance [@Hicke_2024; @Patacca_2022], and @Morris_2016 frame outbreak impact by area affected, host mortality rate and altered stand structure, the three quantities a satellite map has to recover. Yet the operational damage record for Alaska rests on aerial sketch mapping, whose polygons carry coarse positional accuracy, record only what an observer saw that year, and understate dispersed low-severity mortality [@Zwieback_2024; @Hicke_2024].

Satellite remote sensing offers the systematic record that survey flights cannot. The Landsat archive provides four decades of calibrated observation at stand scale [@Wulder_2019], and the established approach extracts temporal features from spectral index trajectories with segmentation algorithms such as LandTrendr [@Kennedy_2010] or continuous change detection [@Zhu_2014], mature enough to have produced a 25-year national record of disturbance and recovery [@White_2017] and to separate defoliators from bark beetles [@Meigs_2011; @Senf_2015; @Meddens_2013]. These methods detect abrupt, stand-replacing disturbance reliably and lose skill exactly where insect damage lives, on partial, gradual change whose trajectories merge with natural forest variation [@Cohen_2017; @Senf_2017], so for bark beetles the mature capability is mapping the red and gray stages of heavily killed stands while low-severity, dispersed mortality remains the recognised frontier [@Hicke_2024; @Marvasti_Zadeh_2023], which is why aerial survey persists and why reviews of the Canadian and United States programmes conclude that remote sensing can augment a survey whose consistency and coverage fall short across a vast forest estate [@Hall_2016; @Housman_2018].

The size of that gap in Alaska is now quantified. @Zwieback_2024 mapped dead spruce at tree scale from 2 m WorldView-2 imagery with a convolutional network at 95 per cent average accuracy, and found that roughly 90 per cent of beetle-killed spruce in their Southcentral study area stood in stands of areal severity below 0.05, while stand-scale Landsat shortwave infrared reflectance change related clearly to severity only above 0.1, so in this landscape of mixed forest with low conifer fractions nearly all mortality sits beneath the detection floor of Landsat change analysis. High-resolution mapping closes that gap at the cost of proprietary imagery, a trade @Hart_2015 measured directly for this beetle, and dating the mortality has been attempted from daily commercial imagery [@Nowak_2026], while Alaska-wide change attribution has relied on intersecting Landsat trends with the same coarse survey perimeters [@Pastick_2018], occurrence models predict beetle habitat rather than damage [@Zabihi_2021], and individual-tree mortality benchmarks exist only outside Alaska [@Khatri_Chhetri_2024].

Deep learning applied to the temporal dimension offers a route below the index-based floor. One-dimensional convolutional networks [@Pelletier_2019] and self-attention models [@Ru_wurm_2020] classify satellite image time series without handcrafted temporal features, joined since by recurrent detectors [@Kong_2018], attention over a convolutional trunk [@Tang_2022] and self-supervised pretraining against label scarcity [@Yuan_2021], surveyed by @Miller_2024. Applied to annual Landsat subsequences over the boreal forest of eastern Canada, TempCNN and Transformer models detected and dated partial and progressive disturbances that LandTrendr-based classification missed, producing the first satellite-derived epidemic maps for the eastern spruce budworm [@Perbet_2024], and whether that transfers from a defoliator in Quebec to a bark beetle in Alaska is unknown, since agent, host, landscape and label regime all differ and reviews caution against porting detection results across pest-host systems [@Kautz_2024]. The European literature on *Ips typographus* (Linnaeus, 1758), the largest body of satellite work on any bark beetle [@Abdullah_2018; @Huo_2021; @Dalponte_2022; @Candotti_2022], targets a tree that fades within one season, where *Dendroctonus*-attacked spruce fade over years, in Alaska from green through red to gray [@Hicke_2024], so the signal here accumulates over time scales a monthly or annual series resolves. What has been missing is a reference severity dataset commensurable with the satellite grid, and that now exists in the tree-scale severity product of @Zwieback_2024, released at 30 to 250 m stand scales, together with sub-metre statewide image mosaics on which further reference labels can be digitised.

This study evaluates deep learning methods and an open radar time series against that reference, and tests whether the climate variables that govern beetle development and survival, set out from the biology at the close of this Introduction, improve what the models can see. It assembles a monthly Sentinel-1 radar series over Southcentral Alaska from June 2017, trains subsequence models [after @Perbet_2024] against stand-scale severity reference data, and measures them against the published shortwave infrared detection floor [@Zwieback_2024]; the annual optical composites built first were set aside for the measured reasons the Methods report. The objectives are to (1) quantify the skill with which an open radar time series estimates stand-scale areal severity of beetle-associated mortality, reported per severity stratum; (2) determine the detectability floor, the lowest severity stratum at which detection skill exceeds a pre-registered threshold, for each method; (3) estimate the year of mortality onset, supervised by onset intervals triangulated between the two label epochs, and quantify its lag relative to the reference record; (4) quantify the contribution of biologically motivated climate variables to detection skill; and (5) reconstruct the annual progression of the outbreak from its 2016 onset through the present across the Matanuska-Susitna Borough application extent, evaluating the reconstruction against the aerial survey archive.

Three hypotheses are tested, all over the complete outbreak trajectory rather than the single dates or two-epoch differences of prior work. Under the null (H0), temporal deep learning models do not exceed the skill of the shortwave infrared change baseline below areal severity of 0.1, and the detection floor of @Zwieback_2024 stands; under the alternative (H1), subsequence models achieve significantly higher detection skill than the baseline within the 0.01 to 0.10 severity stratum, lowering the floor at which freely available imagery can monitor spruce beetle mortality. Under H2, models trained with mortality-onset intervals triangulated between the 2020 and 2023 label epochs date onset more accurately than the same models trained on single-epoch labels. Under H3, models receiving annual climate channels, a summer warmth index anchored on the 17 °C univoltinism threshold [@Hansen_2001], winter minimum temperature, and lagged summer means [@Berg_2006], detect low-severity mortality better than spectrally identical models without them. Estimated onset years are expected to lag true onset by one to two years, as observed for gradual disturbances elsewhere in the boreal [@Perbet_2024], and the severity strata, skill metrics and decision thresholds were fixed by pre-registration before any outcome data were analysed.

The third hypothesis rests on the beetle's biology, and the climate variables it names are defined from three parts of the life cycle, the generation time, the manner of spread and the winter, so the Introduction closes on them. Adult flight in Southcentral Alaska began by the first week of June in two years of trapping, once ambient temperature rose above 12.8 °C, with attack a week or more behind the first flights [@Holsten_2001], in the first half of the period of rapid cambial growth of white spruce [@Hard_1985b]. Whether the brood matures in one year or two is under direct temperature control acting on the fourth larval instar and the prepupa [@Hansen_2001b], and the best predictor of the univoltine proportion at stand level was cumulative hours above 17 °C from 40 to 90 days after peak flight [@Hansen_2001]. The temperature that governs this is that of the phloem rather than the air, since two-year cycles developed on the north and west faces of standing boles at a mean phloem temperature of 10.6 °C while one-year cycles developed on the south faces of the same trees at 16.5 °C [@Werner_1985]. A warm summer therefore halves the generation time without raising fecundity, since egg production did not differ between univoltine, semivoltine and re-emerged parents, and the shorter generation is what raises the rate of spruce mortality in an established outbreak [@Hansen_2003]; warming cannot add a second generation, because an obligate adult diapause requiring cold floors the life cycle at one year [@Bleiker_2019; @Davenport_2024], so the mortality a satellite series records cannot advance faster than an annual increment however warm the summer.

Spread is by threshold and by opportunity rather than along a front. The beetle relies on pheromone-mediated aggregation to raise attack density until it suffices to kill the host [@Jenkins_2014], so mortality accumulates in foci around killed trees, and attack succeeds where host defence is overwhelmed and growth is slow, since trees killed in 1982 carried more completed egg galleries than trees attacked unsuccessfully that year but did not differ from them in diameter [@Hard_1985], and diameter predicted susceptibility only where large size was coupled with slower than average radial growth over the previous five years [@Hard_1983]. Populations build in windthrown and weakened hosts before erupting onto standing stands [@Reynolds_1994], and the eruption is synchronous rather than radial, in Utah at many locations at once [@Jenkins_2014] and in the Southern Rocky Mountains at multiple incipient locations synchronised by regional drivers, with beetle activity correlated only within about five kilometres [@Hart_2017], since *D. rufipennis* released in Alaska were recovered 90 to 300 m from their overwintering sites and at most 600 m away [@Werner_1997]. The regional driver is not temperature alone, because Colorado outbreaks were predicted best by drought, indexed by the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation and summer vapour pressure deficit [@Hart_2014], and initiated in summer, winter and multi-year drought marked by low peak snow water equivalent [@Hart_2017], while in Alaska cold winters held Interior populations at endemic levels until those limits eased [@Holsten_1990], so the summer temperature relationship in the Alaskan record [@Berg_2006; @Sherriff_2011] stands beside a moisture term, and the outbreak is opportunistic in that a population held at endemic level by cold or moisture erupts when the limit lifts, onto hosts already weakened.

The winter sets the last threshold, and it is a depth rather than a temperature. Larvae and adults in Alaska supercooled to about −12 °C in summer and −31 °C in winter, neither stage was freeze tolerant at any time of year, and temperatures beneath the bark of standing spruce showed that only beetles hibernating below the snow line would survive a typical winter [@Miller_1987]; attack concentrates on the lower bole for the same reason, since that part of the stem is often below the snow line [@Hard_1985b; @Holsten_2001]. Winter minimum air temperature therefore bounds survival only for brood above the snow, and the snowpack that shelters the brood is the one whose low peak water equivalent marked the drought-initiated outbreaks of the Southern Rockies [@Hart_2017], so a mild winter and a thin one are not the same event for this insect. Snow depth over a stand follows elevation, canopy closure and terrain, all of which the analysis grid carries, so the overwintering threshold ends as a line on the bole rather than a temperature in the air, and the measurement of the climate the models received begins from that line.

# Materials and methods

Every climate variable the models received was defined from the biology the Introduction closed on, the warmth index from the univoltinism threshold, the winter minimum from the cold to which brood above the snow is exposed, and the lagged summer mean from the delay between a warm summer and the population it produces, so the climate is described first. The sections then place the outbreak in its region and in the aerial survey record, list the inputs, describe the reference labels, the radar record and the optical record that was set aside, define what is fitted, and set out the cross-validation and the tests of the three hypotheses; the label pipeline and the optical record are recorded in full in the supplement under the same section names. All inputs were open, with scripted retrieval, checksums and a provenance manifest beside the code.

## Climate variables

Daily minimum and maximum air temperature from the Daymet version 4 gridded forcings at 1 km [@Thornton_2021], the record standing nearest to the phloem temperature and the snow depth the biology named, were reduced per 90 m stand cell and year to three variables. The summer warmth index was the cumulative degree-hours above 17 °C from June through September, a fixed-window form of the univoltinism predictor of @Hansen_2001; the winter minimum was the lowest daily minimum from November through March, the cold to which brood above the snow line is exposed [@Werner_2006; @Bentz_2010]; and the lagged summer mean was the mean summer temperature two years earlier, following the lagged association in the regional outbreak record [@Berg_2006; @Sherriff_2011]. The regional series was computed for 1990 to 2023 and per-cell rasters were exported at 1 km for each year from 2012.

```{r}
#| label: climate-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
if (!file.exists("../02.inputs/derived/climate_series.csv")) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  tpl_c <- rast("../02.inputs/zwieback-severity/merged_ref_h_c90c.tif")
  bbc <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_c) + 50000, crs = crs(tpl_c)), "EPSG:4326")))
  roi_c <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbc[1], bbc[3], bbc[2], bbc[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")
  yearly <- function(y) {
    smr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-10-01", y))
    tmean <- smr$map(function(img)
      img$select("tmax")$add(img$select("tmin"))$divide(2)$rename("tmean"))
    gdd <- tmean$map(function(img)
      img$subtract(17)$max(0)$multiply(24))$sum()$rename("warmth")
    smean <- tmean$mean()$rename("summer_mean")
    wtr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-11-01", y - 1), sprintf("%d-04-01", y))$
      select("tmin")$min()$rename("winter_min")
    gdd$addBands(smean)$addBands(wtr)$reduceRegion(
      reducer = ee$Reducer$mean(), geometry = roi_c, scale = 1000, maxPixels = 1e10)
  }
  vals <- lapply(1990:2023, function(y) unlist(yearly(y)$getInfo()))
  clim <- data.frame(year = 1990:2023, do.call(rbind, vals))
  clim$summer_mean_lag2 <- c(NA, NA, head(clim$summer_mean, -2))
  dir.create("../02.inputs/derived", showWarnings = FALSE)
  write.csv(clim, "../02.inputs/derived/climate_series.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
clim <- read.csv("../02.inputs/derived/climate_series.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: climate-rasters
#| echo: true
#| output: false
dir.create("../02.inputs/climate", showWarnings = FALSE)
todo_c <- (2012:2023)[!file.exists(sprintf("../02.inputs/climate/clim_%d.tif", 2012:2023))]
if (length(todo_c)) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  tpl_c <- rast("../02.inputs/zwieback-severity/merged_ref_h_c90c.tif")
  bbc <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_c) + 50000, crs = crs(tpl_c)), "EPSG:4326")))
  roi_c <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbc[1], bbc[3], bbc[2], bbc[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")
  for (y in todo_c) {
    smr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-10-01", y))
    tmean <- smr$map(function(img)
      img$select("tmax")$add(img$select("tmin"))$divide(2)$rename("tmean"))
    img <- tmean$map(function(im) im$subtract(17)$max(0)$multiply(24))$sum()$
      rename("warmth")$
      addBands(tmean$mean()$rename("summer_mean"))$
      addBands(dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-11-01", y - 1), sprintf("%d-04-01", y))$
                 select("tmin")$min()$rename("winter_min"))
    url <- img$toFloat()$getDownloadURL(list(region = roi_c, scale = 1000,
                                             crs = "EPSG:32605", format = "GEO_TIFF"))
    old_to <- options(timeout = 600)
    try(download.file(url, sprintf("../02.inputs/climate/clim_%d.tif", y), mode = "wb",
                      quiet = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
    options(old_to)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: climograph-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
if (!file.exists("../02.inputs/derived/climate_monthly.csv")) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  tpl_m <- rast("../02.inputs/climate/clim_2016.tif")
  bbm <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_m), crs = crs(tpl_m)), "EPSG:4326")))
  aoi_m <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbm[1], bbm[3], bbm[2], bbm[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")$
    filterDate("1990-01-01", "2024-01-01")$filterBounds(aoi_m)
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(m) {
    sub <- dm$filter(ee$Filter$calendarRange(m, m, "month"))
    img <- sub$select(c("tmax", "tmin"))$mean()$
      addBands(sub$select("prcp")$mean()$multiply(
        c(31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31)[m])$rename("prcp_month"))
    v <- img$reduceRegion(reducer = ee$Reducer$mean(), geometry = aoi_m,
                          scale = 1000, maxPixels = 1e9, bestEffort = TRUE)$getInfo()
    data.frame(month = m, tmax = v$tmax, tmin = v$tmin, prcp = v$prcp_month)
  }))
  rows$tmean <- (rows$tmax + rows$tmin) / 2
  write.csv(rows, "../02.inputs/derived/climate_monthly.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
clim_m <- read.csv("../02.inputs/derived/climate_monthly.csv")
clim_m$month_name <- month.abb[clim_m$month]
```

@fig-climograph gives the seasonal setting. The warmest month was `r month.name[warm_m$month]`, whose mean daily maximum over 1990 to 2023 was `r sprintf("%.1f", warm_m$tmax)` °C, so an average day of the warmest month did not reach the 17 °C threshold and degree-hours accrue only on the warmer days of the window, which is why the index varies so strongly between years and why a summer a degree above normal shortens the generation [@Hansen_2001]. @fig-climate shows the three variables over 1990 to 2023.

```{r}
#| label: fig-climograph
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Climograph of the study area from Daymet version 4 daily forcings averaged over 1990 to 2023, monthly mean precipitation as bars against monthly mean, maximum and minimum daily air temperature. The horizontal line marks the 17 °C threshold above which spruce beetle development accrues toward a one-year generation, and the shaded band marks June through September, the window over which the summer warmth index integrates. Adult flight occurs in early summer, at the opening of that band."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
base <- floor(min(clim_m$tmin) / 5) * 5
sc <- max(clim_m$prcp) / (max(clim_m$tmax) - base)
ggplot(clim_m, aes(x = month)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 5.5, xmax = 9.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey85", alpha = .55) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = month - .35, xmax = month + .35, ymin = base,
                ymax = base + prcp / sc), fill = "steelblue4", alpha = .75) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 17, linetype = "22", colour = "#C0392B") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.4, y = 18.2, label = "17 °C univoltinism threshold",
           size = 2.5, colour = "#C0392B", hjust = 0) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmax, colour = "Daily maximum"), linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmean, colour = "Daily mean"), linewidth = .6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmin, colour = "Daily minimum"), linewidth = .5) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("Daily maximum" = "#E67E22",
                                       "Daily mean" = "grey20",
                                       "Daily minimum" = "steelblue4")) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Temperature (°C)",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ (. - base) * sc, name = "Precipitation (mm)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(.01, .01)) +
  labs(x = NULL) + th + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: climate-variance
#| echo: true
#| output: false
if (!file.exists("../03.outputs/climate_variance.csv")) {
  cf <- sort(list.files("../02.inputs/climate", pattern = "^clim_[0-9]{4}[.]tif$",
                        full.names = TRUE))
  nm <- c("summer warmth index", "winter minimum", "lagged summer mean")
  cv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(b) {
    st <- rast(lapply(cf, function(x) rast(x)[[b]]))
    v <- terra::extract(st, vect(st_transform(blocks, crs(st))), fun = mean,
                        na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
    v <- v[complete.cases(v), ]
    data.frame(channel = nm[b], blocks = nrow(v), between_year = sd(colMeans(v)),
               between_block = mean(apply(v, 2, sd)))
  }))
  cv$ratio <- cv$between_year / cv$between_block
  write.csv(cv, "../03.outputs/climate_variance.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
climvar <- read.csv("../03.outputs/climate_variance.csv")
cvr <- function(ch) climvar$ratio[climvar$channel == ch]
```

The three annual channels are what the third hypothesis names; the design of 2026-09-09 fits climate values at the radar's monthly step from the same daily forcings, and that fit has not been built. Measured over the `r climvar$blocks[1]` sampled blocks, the summer warmth index varied `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("summer warmth index"))` times as much between years as between blocks, a timing channel, while the winter minimum and the lagged summer mean varied more between blocks within a year than between years, at `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("winter minimum"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("lagged summer mean"))`, so two of the three carry spatial contrast the network can use to tell one stand from another; the warmth index over the blocks in the warmest and the coolest year is Figure S1 in the supplement.

## Study area

The study area was the Southcentral Alaska outbreak region, centred on the Susitna lowlands and the Matanuska-Susitna Valley and bounded by the Talkeetna Mountains and the Alaska Range. Forests are boreal mosaics of white spruce (*Picea glauca* (Moench) Voss), black spruce (*P. mariana* (Mill.) Britton et al.), Alaska birch (*Betula neoalaskana* Sarg.) and trembling aspen (*Populus tremuloides* Michx.), with wetlands and mixed stands in which conifer fractions of 10 to 30% predominate, and the outbreak reached the area around 2016 and had exhausted much of the large white spruce by 2021 [@Zwieback_2024]; the nearest precedent is the Kenai Peninsula outbreak of 1987 to 2000 [@Boucher_2006; @Roynolds_1996]. Training and cross-validation blocks lay in a 39,050 km² confirmatory window around the footprint of the independent severity reference, the Talkeetna to Byers Lake area, which was held out for evaluation, and the Matanuska-Susitna Borough was the application extent for the wall-to-wall maps, summarised per stand of the Borough forest inventory. The design samples one outbreak in one region, so the maps beyond the window are application products the cross-validation does not confirm, and nothing in it estimates transfer to the Kenai Peninsula, to Interior Alaska or to another *Dendroctonus* system. Every map used WGS 84 UTM zone 5N, the grid of the severity reference, and @fig-studyarea locates the blocks and their folds over the terrain with the survey-recorded outbreak footprint.

## Outbreak history

```{r}
#| label: spread-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
if (!file.exists("../03.outputs/survey_spread.csv")) {
  sf_use_s2(FALSE)
  pg <- st_read("../02.inputs/ids-region10/AK_Region10_AllYears.gdb", quiet = TRUE,
                query = paste("SELECT SURVEY_YEAR, ACRES, Shape FROM",
                              "DAMAGE_AREAS_FLAT_AllYears_AK_Rgn10",
                              "WHERE DCA_COMMON_NAME LIKE '%spruce beetle%'"))
  ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(suppressWarnings(st_centroid(st_geometry(pg))), 4326))
  sp <- data.frame(year = pg$SURVEY_YEAR, acres = pg$ACRES, lat = ll[, 2], lon = ll[, 1])
  sp <- sp[complete.cases(sp) & sp$acres > 0, ]
  sp$hectares <- sp$acres * 0.40468564
  write.csv(sp, "../03.outputs/survey_spread.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
spread <- read.csv("../03.outputs/survey_spread.csv")
spread_yr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread, spread$year), function(d)
  data.frame(year = d$year[1], lat = sum(d$lat * d$hectares) / sum(d$hectares),
             kha = sum(d$hectares) / 1000)))
spread_fit <- lm(lat ~ year, spread_yr)
spread_cap <- paste0(
  "Spruce beetle damage recorded by the Alaska aerial detection survey, ",
  min(spread$year), " to ", max(spread$year), ", from all ",
  format(nrow(spread), big.mark = ","), " polygons the survey attributes to the ",
  "agent with a recorded area. (a) Damage area by quarter-degree latitude band ",
  "and survey year, on a square-root colour scale so the smaller years remain ",
  "visible. (b) The area-weighted mean latitude of damage in each year, sized by ",
  "the area recorded that year, with a least-squares line and its interval. The ",
  "survey records where observers flew, so the recorded centre reflects survey ",
  "effort as well as beetle activity."
)
```

The aerial detection survey has recorded spruce beetle damage in Alaska since 1997, and @fig-spread draws its whole span. Across `r nrow(spread_yr)` survey years the area-weighted mean latitude of recorded damage moved north by `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(spread_fit)[2] * diff(range(spread_yr$year)))` degrees, about `r sprintf("%.0f", coef(spread_fit)[2] * diff(range(spread_yr$year)) * 111)` km \[F(1, `r spread_fit$df.residual`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(spread_fit)$fstatistic[1])`, p = `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(spread_fit)$coefficients[2, 4])`, R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(spread_fit)$r.squared)`\], a drift rather than a march, since the trend explained under a quarter of the year-to-year variance, the survey records where observers flew, and the mass at the start of the record is the Kenai Peninsula outbreak while the mass at the end is the Susitna lowlands, so the centre of recorded damage moved between two events rather than one population tracked as it moved. @fig-survey-map draws the same record on the ground.


```{r}
#| label: fig-spread
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: !expr spread_cap
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.4
spread$band <- floor(spread$lat * 4) / 4
sp_grid <- aggregate(hectares ~ band + year, spread, sum)
ps_a <- ggplot(sp_grid, aes(year, band, fill = hectares / 1000)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt", name = "kha") +
  labs(title = "(a) Recorded damage by latitude", x = NULL,
       y = "Latitude (degrees north)") + th
ps_b <- ggplot(spread_yr, aes(year, lat)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#C0392B", fill = "#C0392B",
              alpha = .15, linewidth = .5, formula = y ~ x) +
  geom_point(aes(size = kha), colour = "steelblue4", alpha = .85) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(.8, 4.5), name = "kha") +
  labs(title = "(b) Area-weighted mean latitude", x = NULL,
       y = "Latitude (degrees north)") + th
ps_a / ps_b
```

The study drew on `r nrow(inp)` input datasets in four roles (@tbl-inputs). Reference data were the crown delineations digitised on the two State of Alaska mosaic epochs, seeded by the released labels and network of @Zwieback_2024, and that study's independent severity rasters; predictor data were the Sentinel-1 radar series, with the annual Sentinel-2 and Landsat composites built first and set aside; terrain and conifer fraction [@Macander_2022] conditioned sampling; and the aerial detection survey polygons and their flown-area footprints stratified the sample and separated surveyed absence from non-survey.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inputs
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Input datasets, their roles, and access terms."
fmt_tbl(inp)
```

## Training data

Stand-scale areal severity of beetle-associated dead spruce for the Talkeetna to Byers Lake area in 2021, derived by @Zwieback_2024 from a convolutional network applied to WorldView-2 imagery and therefore a model product with its own documented error rather than ground truth, was used at its three released stand scales solely for independent evaluation, and its metadata alone were inspected before pre-registration.

```{r}
#| label: severity-metadata
#| echo: true
sev <- lapply(sprintf("../02.inputs/zwieback-severity/merged_ref_h_c%sc.tif", c(30, 90, 250)), rast)
data.frame(
  file = vapply(sev, function(r) basename(sources(r)), ""),
  resolution = vapply(sev, function(r) paste(round(res(r)), collapse = " x "), ""),
  ncell = vapply(sev, ncell, numeric(1)),
  crs = vapply(sev, function(r) st_crs(crs(r))$Name, "")
)
```

## Crown labels

```{r}
#| label: label-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
pairs <- read.csv("../03.outputs/label_pairs.csv")
crown_m <- read.csv("../03.outputs/crown_net_metrics.csv")
best <- crown_m[which.max(crown_m$val_iou), ]
op <- read.csv("../03.outputs/crown_operating_point.csv")
tq <- read.csv("../03.outputs/triage_queue.csv")
```

Reference labels were dead spruce crowns digitised over the 160 sampled blocks on the State of Alaska mosaics of 2020, at 0.5 m, and 2023, at 0.3 m, at which a single crown is many pixels wide; the mosaics are licensed Maxar imagery, so the pixels were processed locally and never redistributed, and the study publishes only the derived crowns and severity fractions, as @Zwieback_2024 did. Labelling ran in four stages, adapted from @Zwieback_2024 for the pre-labelling and from @Khatri_Chhetri_2024 for the triage. The released dead-spruce network of @Zwieback_2024 was adapted from the seven bands of its WorldView-2 training imagery to the four the mosaics carry and fine-tuned on that study's published crown delineations, `r format(sum(pairs$crowns), big.mark = ",")` crowns over `r nrow(pairs)` delineation areas, keeping the epoch that validated best on held-out areas, at a pixel recall of `r sprintf("%.2f", best$val_recall)` and precision of `r sprintf("%.2f", best$val_precision)`. Its candidates were refined into crown polygons with DeepForest [@Weinstein_2019] and the Segment Anything Model [@Wu_2023] and written per block and epoch at a probability threshold of 0.5, `r format(sum(tq$candidates), big.mark = ",")` candidate polygons at a median of `r median(tq$candidates)` per block, for two annotators to accept, edit or reject in QGIS with a third adjudicating. Accepted crowns were rasterised to the fraction of each 30 m and 90 m stand cell they cover, the areal severity, and classified at the pre-registered breaks, and comparing the two epochs gave each crown a state, dead by 2020, died between 2020 and 2023, or alive through 2023, which supplied the interval-censored onset labels and returned to triage any crown dead in 2020 and alive in 2023. The published labels of @Zwieback_2024 joined the training pool within their own delineation areas with cuts at 2018 and 2021, while that study's severity rasters took no part in labelling; mortality agent was inferred from context, and dead spruce fully hidden under closed deciduous canopy are absent from the labels [@Zwieback_2024]. The tuning pairs, the network and its operating point, the queue and the planned separability test are in the supplement under Crown labels, Crown network, Triage queue and Spectral separability.


## Survey polygons

Sketch-mapped damage polygons for Alaska, all survey years, were not used as labels, because positional accuracy is coarse, low-severity damage is under-recorded, and the intensity attribute counts faded trees per treed area, which is not commensurable with pixel-fraction severity [@Zwieback_2024]. They stratified the block sample by recorded damage history and, through the flown-area footprints, distinguished surveyed absence from non-survey; annual extent is tabulated below as descriptive context.

```{r}
#| label: ids-context
#| echo: true
st_layers("../02.inputs/ids-region10/AK_Region10_AllYears.gdb")
ids_sql <- function(sql) {
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  gdal_utils("vectortranslate", "../02.inputs/ids-region10/AK_Region10_AllYears.gdb", tmp,
             options = c("-dialect", "SQLite", "-sql", sql))
  read.csv(tmp)
}
sb <- ids_sql('
  SELECT SURVEY_YEAR, DCA_CODE, DCA_COMMON_NAME,
         COUNT(*) AS n_polygons, SUM(ACRES) AS acres
  FROM DAMAGE_AREAS_FLAT_AllYears_AK_Rgn10
  WHERE DCA_COMMON_NAME LIKE "%spruce beetle%"
  GROUP BY SURVEY_YEAR, DCA_CODE')
aggregate(cbind(n_polygons = sb$n_polygons, hectares = round(sb$acres * 0.40468564)),
          by = list(agent = sb$DCA_COMMON_NAME), FUN = sum)
data.frame(year = sb$SURVEY_YEAR[sb$DCA_CODE == 11009],
           n_polygons = sb$n_polygons[sb$DCA_CODE == 11009],
           hectares = round(sb$acres[sb$DCA_CODE == 11009] * 0.40468564))
```

## Radar record

```{r}
#| label: radar-record-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
s1_scenes <- read.csv("../03.outputs/s1_rtc_scene_means.csv")
seen <- lapply(split(s1_scenes$block, s1_scenes$track), unique)
s1_blocks <- c(only_131 = length(setdiff(seen[["131"]], seen[["160"]])),
               both = length(intersect(seen[["131"]], seen[["160"]])),
               only_160 = length(setdiff(seen[["160"]], seen[["131"]])))
s1_nscene <- tapply(s1_scenes$scene_id, s1_scenes$track, function(x) length(unique(x)))
s1_first <- min(as.Date(s1_scenes$date[s1_scenes$track == 131]))
s1_floor30 <- read.csv("../03.outputs/radar_noise_floor_undamaged_30m.csv")
s1_ref <- read.csv("../03.outputs/radar_noise_floor.csv")
floor30 <- function(what, b, p)
  s1_floor30[[what]][s1_floor30$processing == p & s1_floor30$band == b]
ref_db <- function(q) s1_ref$value[s1_ref$quantity == q]
yr_floor <- function(b, p = "mt_filtered") floor30("year_to_year_median_db", b, p)
rep_floor <- function(b, p = "mt_filtered") floor30("repeatability_median_db", b, p)
removed <- function(b) 100 * (1 - yr_floor(b) / yr_floor(b, "unfiltered"))
canopy_ratio <- c(VV = ref_db("windthrow_vv_db") / yr_floor("VV"),
                  VH = ref_db("windthrow_vh_db") / yr_floor("VH"))
s1val <- read.csv("../03.outputs/s1gbm_validation.csv")
s1_cube_files <- list.files("../02.inputs/derived/s1_cube_30m",
                            pattern = "^SENTINEL-1_RTC_.*[.]tif$")
s1_cube_dates <- as.Date(unique(regmatches(
  s1_cube_files, regexpr("[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}", s1_cube_files))))
```

The predictor record was Sentinel-1 C-band radar over the 160 sampled blocks from June 2017 onward, with two polarisations, VV, sent and received vertically, and VH, received horizontally, which returns more from the canopy than from the ground. Radar passes through cloud, which is what limits optical observation in Southcentral Alaska, so a monthly step was available where the optical record supported an annual one. Scenes came from the Planetary Computer's terrain corrected collection, `sentinel-1-rtc`, in which the return is corrected for the slope and aspect of the ground [@Small_2011] so that terrain does not read as forest, at 10 m sampling; the comparison against Earth Engine's uncorrected collection, where the first extraction was made, is in the supplement under Radar record.

Two descending orbits, 131 and 160, crossed the blocks, and only orbit 131 entered the series, because it saw every block, `r s1_blocks[["only_131"]]` of them alone and `r s1_blocks[["both"]]` together with orbit 160, which saw `r s1_blocks[["only_160"]]` alone; the two agreed over the shared blocks on the corrected record, measured in the supplement, and orbit 160 was kept as a repeatability check. The record began on `r format(s1_first, "%d %B %Y")`, because earlier scenes over this frame carry VV alone, and holds `r s1_nscene[["131"]]` scenes on orbit 131.

Each scene was held on a 30 m grid nested three by three inside the 90 m stand cells, so the severity labels joined both records without resampling; 10 m is the product's sampling and not the instrument's resolution, and 30 m was the finest grid that did not oversample it. No layover and shadow mask was applied on the low relief of the Susitna lowlands, an omission the Limitations record.

Every date was kept, because the multi-temporal speckle filter of the Sentinel-1 Toolbox after @Quegan_2000, implemented in `05.scripts/15_mt_speckle_filter.py`, takes its noise reduction from the length of the series; speckle is the grainy noise of a radar image. Each date keeps its own local mean over a 3 by 3 window, the ratios of every image to its local mean are averaged across all dates, and each date's mean is multiplied back, so real change between dates stays while the speckle cancels across the stack. @fig-filter shows one block on one date before and after.

```{python}
#| label: filter-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| python.reticulate: false
#| engine.path: /opt/local/bin/python3
import os, csv, zipfile
import numpy as np


def block_vv(path, date, block):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as zf:
        dates, blocks = np.load(zf.open("date.npy")), np.load(zf.open("block.npy"))
        with zf.open("stack.npy") as f:
            np.lib.format.read_magic(f)
            shape = np.lib.format.read_array_header_1_0(f)[0]
            n = shape[3] * shape[4]
            i = np.flatnonzero(dates == date)[0] * shape[1] * shape[2]
            i += np.flatnonzero(blocks == block)[0]
            f.seek(f.tell() + 4 * i * n)
            return np.frombuffer(f.read(4 * n), dtype="float32").reshape(shape[3:])


if not os.path.exists("../03.outputs/filter_effect_block.csv"):
    with zipfile.ZipFile("../02.inputs/derived/s1_block_stack_30m.npz") as zf:
        dates, blocks = np.load(zf.open("date.npy")), np.load(zf.open("block.npy"))
        x0, y1 = np.load(zf.open("x0.npy")), np.load(zf.open("y1.npy"))
    date = next(d for d in dates if d.startswith("2019-07"))
    k = next(i for i, b in enumerate(blocks) if not np.isnan(
        block_vv("../02.inputs/derived/s1_block_stack_30m.npz", date, b)).any())
    cells = zip(
        block_vv("../02.inputs/derived/s1_block_stack_30m.npz", date, blocks[k]).ravel(),
        block_vv("../02.inputs/derived/s1_block_stack_30m_mtfiltered.npz", date,
                 blocks[k]).ravel())
    with open("../03.outputs/filter_effect_block.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.writer(fh)
        w.writerow(["block", "date", "x0", "y1", "before", "after"])
        w.writerows([blocks[k], date, x0[k], y1[k], b, a] for b, a in cells)
```

```{r}
#| label: filter-effect
#| echo: true
#| output: false
fe <- read.csv("../03.outputs/filter_effect_block.csv")
n <- sqrt(nrow(fe))
fe_r <- rast(nrows = n, ncols = n, xmin = fe$x0[1], xmax = fe$x0[1] + 30 * n,
             ymin = fe$y1[1] - 30 * n, ymax = fe$y1[1], crs = "EPSG:32605",
             nlyrs = 2, names = c("before", "after"))
values(fe_r) <- 10 * log10(as.matrix(fe[, c("before", "after")]))
fe_lim <- range(values(fe_r), na.rm = TRUE)
fe_sd <- apply(values(fe_r), 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
filter_cap <- paste0(
  "One block on one date before and after the multi-temporal speckle filter, ",
  "VV backscatter in decibels at ", res(fe_r)[1], " m over the ", n, " by ", n,
  " cells of block ", as.integer(sub("block_", "", fe$block[1])), " on ",
  format(as.Date(fe$date[1]), "%d %B %Y"), ", on one colour range. The filter ",
  "takes each date's ratio to its own local mean in a 3 by 3 window and ",
  "averages those ratios across every date in the series, so the outer ring ",
  "of cells, where the window has no neighbour, is left empty. The standard ",
  "deviation across the block's cells fell from ", sprintf("%.2f", fe_sd[["before"]]),
  " to ", sprintf("%.2f", fe_sd[["after"]]), " dB. WGS 84 UTM zone 5N ",
  "(EPSG:32605), graticule in m."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-filter
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: !expr filter_cap
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
fe_panel <- function(lyr, title, legend) {
  tm_shape(fe_r[[lyr]]) +
    tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "viridis", limits = fe_lim),
              col.legend = legend) +
    map_frame(title, legend = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"), n.x = 3, n.y = 3)
}
tmap_arrange(
  fe_panel("before", "(a) Before the filter", tm_legend_hide()),
  fe_panel("after", "(b) After the filter",
           tm_legend(title = "VV (dB)", reverse = TRUE, height = 6)),
  ncol = 2, outer.margins = 0.01
)
```

The chain was checked against the Sentinel-1 Global Backscatter Model [@Bauer_Marschallinger_2021], an independent processor's mean backscatter of 2016 and 2017 over the same ground, and across the `r s1val$n_blocks[1]` blocks the two agreed in pattern at a correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", s1val$pearson_r[s1val$band == "VV"])` in VV and `r sprintf("%.3f", s1val$pearson_r[s1val$band == "VH"])` in VH; their levels differ by `r sprintf("%.2f", s1val$offset_db[s1val$band == "VV"])` dB in VV and `r sprintf("%.2f", s1val$offset_db[s1val$band == "VH"])` dB in VH, an offset decomposed in the supplement.

The noise floor was measured where nothing had happened, on the `r unique(s1_floor30$blocks)` blocks in which the aerial survey never recorded damage, at 30 m, June through September, before and after the filter. The year-to-year spread of one cell's monthly mean for the same calendar month, which is what a multi-year change has to clear, fell with the filter from `r sprintf("%.2f", yr_floor("VV", "unfiltered"))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", yr_floor("VV"))` dB in VV and from `r sprintf("%.2f", yr_floor("VH", "unfiltered"))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", yr_floor("VH"))` dB in VH. Against the total canopy removal that @R_etschi_2019 measured by windthrow, `r sprintf("%.2f", ref_db("windthrow_vv_db"))` dB in VV and `r sprintf("%.2f", ref_db("windthrow_vh_db"))` dB in VH (their page 11), the filtered floor gave ratios of `r sprintf("%.2f", canopy_ratio[["VV"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", canopy_ratio[["VH"]])`, so at a single 30 m cell in a single year total canopy removal sat at the floor and the low-severity mortality this study exists to detect sat below it. Two things keep that from being the model's floor, which has not been measured, in that a 90 m stand cell holds nine 30 m cells and the model reads a trajectory across many months and years rather than one difference; what the model can detect is what the pre-registered tests measure.

From the filtered stack the series was composited to calendar month and written as a local cube for the sits package, `r length(s1_cube_files)` rasters holding VV and VH, one per band per month over `r length(s1_cube_dates)` months from `r format(min(s1_cube_dates), "%B %Y")` to `r format(max(s1_cube_dates), "%B %Y")`. The models receive the Kennaugh elements K0 and K1, the sum and the difference of the VV and VH intensities after @Hechtl_2025, who ranked them first and second in their own importance analysis, formed inside sits and converted to decibels afterwards. @fig-season draws the cube's July and November of one year block by block, the seasonal cycle the Limitations return to.

```{r}
#| label: season-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
k0_blocks <- function(month) {
  r <- rast(sprintf("../02.inputs/derived/s1_cube_30m/SENTINEL-1_RTC_TBL01_%s_2020-%02d-01.tif",
                    c("VV", "VH"), month))
  sapply(seq_len(nrow(blocks)), function(i)
    10 * log10(sum(global(crop(r, vect(blocks[i, ])), "mean", na.rm = TRUE)$mean)))
}
blocks$k0_jul <- k0_blocks(7)
blocks$k0_nov <- k0_blocks(11)
k0_lim <- range(c(blocks$k0_jul, blocks$k0_nov), na.rm = TRUE)
season_cap <- paste0(
  "K0, the sum of the VV and VH intensities in decibels, per sampled block from ",
  "the filtered monthly cube, (a) July and (b) November 2020, on one colour ",
  "range from ", sprintf("%.1f", k0_lim[1]), " to ", sprintf("%.1f", k0_lim[2]),
  " dB. Each square is the mean of the 30 m cells inside one block, drawn ",
  "larger than the block. Across the ",
  sum(complete.cases(blocks$k0_jul, blocks$k0_nov)), " blocks holding both ",
  "months, July sat ", sprintf("%.2f", mean(blocks$k0_jul - blocks$k0_nov,
                                             na.rm = TRUE)),
  " dB above November. The dashed orange rectangle is the confirmatory study ",
  "window. WGS 84 UTM zone 5N (EPSG:32605), graticule in km."
)
```

## Satellite composites

The optical record was built first, between 2026-08-11 and 2026-09-08, and set aside as a predictor on 2026-09-09 for the reason measured below. Annual July to August composites were built in Google Earth Engine [@Gorelick_2017] on the 90 m reference grid, Sentinel-2 surface reflectance for 2016 to 2025 with cloud masked by Cloud Score+ at 0.40 [@Pasquarella_2023] and Landsat 8 for 2014 to 2018 as the pre-outbreak baseline, harmonised across the two sensors as in @Perbet_2024, then split into a data cube for the sits package [@Simoes_2021] holding red, near infrared and two shortwave infrared bands at one date per year; the scene lists, the clear-observation counts, which were low in the Landsat years, and the cube checks are in the supplement under Composite assembly and Analysis cube.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
if (!file.exists("../03.outputs/block_trajectories.csv")) {
  cube_files <- list.files("../02.inputs/derived/sits_cube", pattern = "^SENTINEL.*\\.tif$",
                           full.names = TRUE)
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cube_files, function(f) {
    parts <- strsplit(basename(f), "_")[[1]]
    v <- terra::extract(rast(f), vect(blocks), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
    data.frame(block = blocks$block, band = parts[4],
               year = as.integer(substr(parts[5], 1, 4)), value = as.numeric(v[, 1]))
  }))
  write.csv(rows, "../03.outputs/block_trajectories.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
traj <- read.csv("../03.outputs/block_trajectories.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-step
#| echo: true
#| output: false
step_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(traj, traj$band), function(d) {
  m <- aggregate(value ~ year, d, median)
  m <- m[order(m$year), ]
  st <- diff(m$value)
  yrs <- m$year[-1]
  data.frame(band = d$band[1], boundary = st[yrs == 2019],
             other_median = median(abs(st[yrs != 2019])),
             ratio = abs(st[yrs == 2019]) / median(abs(st[yrs != 2019])))
}))
```

```{r}
#| label: step-by-damage
#| echo: true
#| output: false
step_blk <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(traj, list(traj$block, traj$band)), function(d) {
  d <- d[order(d$year), ]
  i <- which(d$year == 2019)
  if (!length(i) || i == 1) return(NULL)
  data.frame(block = d$block[1], band = d$band[1], step = d$value[i] - d$value[i - 1])
}))
step_blk <- merge(step_blk, data.frame(block = blocks$block, damage = blocks$damage), by = "block")
step_blk <- step_blk[!is.na(step_blk$step), ]
step_test <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(step_blk, step_blk$band), function(d) {
  a <- d$step[d$damage]; b <- d$step[!d$damage]
  w <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(a, b))
  data.frame(band = d$band[1], med_damage = median(a), med_none = median(b),
             n_damage = length(a), n_none = length(b), W = unname(w$statistic), p = w$p.value)
}))
```

The record was set aside because of the join between its two sensors. The step between 2018, the last Landsat year, and 2019, the first Sentinel-2 year, was the largest year-to-year change in the twelve-year record in both shortwave infrared bands, where dead spruce are brightest, `r sprintf("%.1f", step_tab$ratio[step_tab$band == "B12"])` times the median step in shortwave infrared 2 and `r sprintf("%.1f", step_tab$ratio[step_tab$band == "B11"])` times in shortwave infrared 1, and it did not differ between the `r step_test$n_damage[1]` blocks with survey-recorded damage and the `r step_test$n_none[1]` without, `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_damage[step_test$band == "B12"])` against `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_none[step_test$band == "B12"])` reflectance \[W = `r sprintf("%.0f", step_test$W[step_test$band == "B12"])`, p = `r sprintf("%.2f", step_test$p[step_test$band == "B12"])`\], so the step was the instrument and not the outbreak. The pre-registered baseline straddled it, no cross-sensor correction [@Zhang_2018; @Chastain_2019; @Claverie_2018; @Ju_2025] had been applied, and the amendment of 2026-09-09 moved the predictor record to radar rather than correcting the join.


## Subsequence sampling

Following @Perbet_2024, the record is cut into fixed-length subsequences, seven to ten years on the annual record as pre-registered and a span the amendment of 2026-09-09 fixes on the monthly one. The onset date sits at a randomised position within each labelled window, never the first step, so the models learn the shape of the trajectory rather than a calendar position [@Iwana_2021], and every labelled stand is observed from June 2017 through the present, so the models recognise a trajectory rather than a change from a pre-outbreak state, as @Hechtl_2025 did. Each labelled cell contributes its severity fraction, its onset interval, credited anywhere within the bracket, and the climate values at the same monthly step, undisturbed stands from surveyed-absence areas complete the set, and @fig-design draws the sampling scheme and the two-head design as pre-registered.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The subsequence sampling scheme and the two-head design, both as pre-registered. (a) The annual record 2014 to 2025 is cut into fixed-length subsequences of seven to ten years, four of which are drawn as examples; the onset year sits at a randomised position inside each window and never at its first year, so the network learns the shape of the trajectory rather than a calendar position. The shaded band is the censoring interval for a stand alive at the 2020 label epoch and dead by the 2023 one; a stand already dead in 2020 carries an open bracket before that epoch instead, which is the case for the first and third subsequences drawn. (b) One convolutional trunk over the temporal axis feeds two heads, severity and relative onset year, and the onset head is scored against the bracket rather than a point, which is the loss H2 is defined by."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.2
yrs <- 2014:2025
win <- data.frame(id = factor(1:4), start = c(2014, 2016, 2015, 2018),
                  len = c(8, 10, 7, 8), onset = c(2018, 2021, 2019, 2022))
win$end <- win$start + win$len - 1
pa <- ggplot(win) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2020, xmax = 2023, ymin = 0.4, ymax = 4.6,
           fill = "grey88") +
  annotate("text", x = 2021.5, y = 4.85, label = "censoring bracket",
           size = 2.5, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, y = as.numeric(id),
                   yend = as.numeric(id)), linewidth = 3.2,
               colour = "steelblue4", alpha = .8, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = onset, y = as.numeric(id)), size = 2.1,
             colour = "#C0392B") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = yrs, limits = c(2013.6, 2025.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = paste("subsequence", 1:4),
                     limits = c(0.4, 5.1)) +
  labs(title = "(a) Subsequence sampling", x = NULL, y = NULL) + th

box <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2.35, 3.7, 5.05, 5.05),
  y = c(3, 3, 3, 3.8, 2.2),
  lab = c("input\n7 to 10 years\nx 4 bands +\n3 climate", "temporal\nconvolutions",
          "dense\nlayers", "severity\nhead", "onset\nhead"))
seg <- data.frame(x = c(1.5, 2.85, 4.2, 4.2), xend = c(1.85, 3.2, 4.55, 4.55),
                  y = c(3, 3, 3, 3), yend = c(3, 3, 3.8, 2.2))
pb <- ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = box, aes(x, y), width = 1.0, height = 1.05,
            fill = "grey95", colour = "grey45", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(data = box, aes(x, y, label = lab), size = 2.4, lineheight = .95) +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = yend),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(.14, "cm")), linewidth = .35,
               colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.05, y = 1.45,
           label = "scored against the bracket, not a point",
           size = 2.3, colour = "#C0392B") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 5.75)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1.2, 4.5)) +
  labs(title = "(b) Two-head design", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  th + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
             panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.border = element_blank())

pa / pb + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15))
```

## Architectures

Two networks are applied on identical inputs, following @Perbet_2024. TempCNN applies one-dimensional convolutions along the time axis without pooling [@Pelletier_2019], followed by dense layers and task heads, and the Transformer encoder weights every observation of the series against every other by self-attention [@Ru_wurm_2020]. In boreal disturbance classification TempCNN matched or exceeded a LandTrendr and random forest workflow, with its largest margins on partial disturbance, and the Transformer came within two accuracy points of it [@Perbet_2024].

## Baseline model

The comparator for the first hypothesis was restated by the unsigned amendment of 2026-09-09. The pre-registered null model was the stand-scale change analysis that defines the current floor [@Zwieback_2024], pre-outbreak minus post-outbreak summer shortwave-infrared reflectance per stand cell, and that difference cannot be formed on a record that begins after the outbreak did. The comparator is therefore the published floor itself, the severity of 0.1 above which @Zwieback_2024 found that change related clearly to severity, which is the quantity the title claims to lower; a radar change baseline needs a pre-outbreak radar state and a single-date radar classifier would test the time series rather than the floor, so both were rejected. The annual random forest mapping of @Bright_2020, trained on high-resolution crowns aggregated to percent dead at 30 m, is the published state of the art for the task and enters as a comparator, and dense time series have recovered subtle change in mountain pine beetle and spruce beetle systems before [@Ye_2021].

## Model training

Both networks are trained on identical inputs with two heads, a severity output classified at the pre-registered breaks with the continuous fraction kept for regression, and a relative onset output, through the sits package [@Simoes_2021] on its torch backend, with Adam, cross-entropy losses, dropout and weight decay, and hyperparameters tuned on a validation split held apart from every test block. The onset head is a discrete-time formulation over the censoring bracket after the neural survival model of @Gensheimer_2019, which scores an interval label without inventing a point within it. The ablations for the second and third hypotheses retrain the same architecture with point onset labels in place of intervals and with the climate values removed; depths, loss weights and schedules are fixed at pre-registration, and configurations and logs are archived with the code.

## Pipeline validation

```{r}
#| label: pipeline-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
endmember_tbl <- read.csv("../03.outputs/endmember.csv")
em_sw <- endmember_tbl[endmember_tbl$estimator == "change" & endmember_tbl$band == "swir16", ]
syn_recall <- read.csv("../03.outputs/synthetic_severity_recall.csv")
rec_m <- syn_recall[syn_recall$endmember == "measured", ]
```

Before any label was scored, the optical pipeline was tested end to end on mortality injected into real trajectories of the analysis cube, a severity-weighted mix of each cell's own live spectrum and a dead-crown endmember faded in over two years after @Hicke_2024. The endmember, the change in reflectance from a fully live to a fully dead stand, was measured by regressing each cell's change from its pre-outbreak state on the fraction the delineated crowns of @Zwieback_2024 cover, `r sprintf("%+.3f", em_sw$endmember)` in the 1.6 µm shortwave infrared (95 per cent confidence interval `r sprintf("%+.3f", em_sw$ci_low)` to `r sprintf("%+.3f", em_sw$ci_high)`, `r format(em_sw$n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells). A temporal convolutional network tested on `r format(sum(rec_m$n), big.mark = ",")` held-out synthetic samples recovered the injected decline only above a severity of 0.1, recall `r sprintf("%.2f", rec_m$recall[rec_m$stratum == "(0.1,0.2]"])` in the 0.1 to 0.2 stratum and at most `r sprintf("%.2f", max(rec_m$recall[rec_m$stratum %in% c("[0,0.01]", "(0.01,0.03]", "(0.03,0.05]", "(0.05,0.1]")]))` below it, on a seven-way assignment that does not estimate the fixed-precision detection H1 is scored by; the calibration and the test are in the supplement.


## Model evaluation

Evaluation uses block spatial cross-validation, the 160 blocks assigned wholly to eight folds, to limit leakage through spatial autocorrelation [@Perbet_2024; @Roberts_2017; @Karasiak_2021], and skill is reported per severity stratum. Detection is summarised by full confusion matrices with user's and producer's accuracy per class [@Olofsson_2014; @Stehman_2019], with the spatial unit of assessment stated [@Stehman_2011], and the kappa coefficient is not reported [@Foody_2020]. The primary metric is recall at a fixed precision of 0.90 in the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, because precision and recall describe a rare positive class where a receiver operating characteristic does not [@Saito_2015; @Sofaer_2019]. Severity regression is summarised by root-mean-square error, relative RMSE normalised by the stratum mean of the reference severity, mean absolute error, and Theil's U inequality coefficient with its bias, variance and covariance decomposition [@Gupta_2009; @Hodson_2021], and onset dating by mean absolute error in years, all with fold-wise dispersion. Hypothesis tests are paired and fold-wise, a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank on the primary metric difference with a block-bootstrap confidence interval [@Demsar_2006], supported by McNemar's test on paired cell-level detections [@Dietterich_1998]. H1 is tested by paired comparison of deep and baseline skill across folds within the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, H2 by an ablation retraining the same architectures with single-epoch labels in place of triangulated onset intervals, compared on onset mean absolute error, and H3 by the equivalent ablation on inputs, climate-augmented against spectral-only models, on the primary detection metric, and the three form one Holm-corrected family. The severity product of @Zwieback_2024 provides a fully independent evaluation in the Talkeetna to Byers Lake footprint, using only fold models whose training blocks exclude it, because that study's crown labels participate in training, and the reconstructed annual outbreak progression is evaluated by areal correspondence with annual aerial survey extent [@Perbet_2024; @Perbet_2025] and reported as descriptive.

```{r}

#| echo: true
#| eval: false

strata <- c(0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1)
```

### Evaluation harness

Every metric and test above is implemented below, before any label exists, and exercised on constructed inputs whose answers follow from their construction, with the chunk stopping if any disagrees.

```{r}
#| label: eval-harness
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Recall at a fixed precision. The operating point is chosen on the calibration
# data and applied unchanged elsewhere, per the pre-registration: choosing it on
# the test fold would report the best threshold in hindsight.
threshold_at_precision <- function(score, positive, target = 0.90) {
  ord <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)
  tp <- cumsum(positive[ord])
  prec <- tp / seq_along(tp)
  ok <- which(prec >= target & tp > 0)
  if (!length(ok)) return(Inf)          # target precision unreachable
  score[ord][max(ok)]
}
recall_at_threshold <- function(score, positive, thr) {
  if (!sum(positive)) return(NA_real_)
  if (!is.finite(thr)) return(0)
  sum(score >= thr & positive) / sum(positive)
}

# Confusion matrix with user's accuracy (correct / predicted as that class) and
# producer's accuracy (correct / reference of that class).
confusion <- function(truth, pred, lev = sort(unique(c(truth, pred)))) {
  m <- table(pred = factor(pred, lev), truth = factor(truth, lev))
  d <- diag(m)
  data.frame(class = lev,
             n_reference = as.integer(colSums(m)),
             n_predicted = as.integer(rowSums(m)),
             users = ifelse(rowSums(m) > 0, d / rowSums(m), NA_real_),
             producers = ifelse(colSums(m) > 0, d / colSums(m), NA_real_),
             row.names = NULL)
}

rmse <- function(obs, pred) sqrt(mean((pred - obs)^2))
mae <- function(obs, pred) mean(abs(pred - obs))
rrmse <- function(obs, pred) rmse(obs, pred) / mean(obs)

# Theil's U inequality coefficient with the bias, variance and covariance
# proportions of mean squared error, which sum to one by construction. The
# decomposition separates systematic offset from unexplained scatter.
theil <- function(obs, pred) {
  mse <- mean((pred - obs)^2)
  if (mse == 0) return(c(U = 0, bias = 0, variance = 0, covariance = 0))
  n <- length(obs)
  sd_p <- sqrt(mean((pred - mean(pred))^2))     # population sd, so the
  sd_o <- sqrt(mean((obs - mean(obs))^2))       # proportions sum to one
  r <- if (sd_p == 0 || sd_o == 0) 0 else cor(obs, pred)
  c(U = sqrt(mse) / (sqrt(mean(obs^2)) + sqrt(mean(pred^2))),
    bias = (mean(pred) - mean(obs))^2 / mse,
    variance = (sd_p - sd_o)^2 / mse,
    covariance = 2 * (1 - r) * sd_p * sd_o / mse)
}

# Paired fold-wise test: one-sided Wilcoxon signed rank on the per-fold
# difference, with a block bootstrap over folds for the interval. Resampling
# folds rather than cells is what keeps spatial dependence inside a resampling
# unit.
paired_fold_test <- function(diff, alternative = "greater", B = 10000,
                             seed = 20260812) {
  p <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(diff, alternative = alternative)$p.value)
  set.seed(seed)
  bs <- replicate(B, mean(sample(diff, length(diff), replace = TRUE)))
  c(mean_diff = mean(diff), p_value = p,
    ci_low = unname(quantile(bs, 0.025)),
    ci_high = unname(quantile(bs, 0.975)))
}

# McNemar on paired cell-level detections: only the discordant pairs carry
# information about which method is better.
mcnemar_paired <- function(correct_a, correct_b) {
  b <- sum(correct_a & !correct_b); c_ <- sum(!correct_a & correct_b)
  if (b + c_ == 0) return(c(b = 0, c = 0, p_value = 1))
  c(b = b, c = c_,
    p_value = suppressWarnings(
      mcnemar.test(matrix(c(sum(correct_a & correct_b), b, c_,
                            sum(!correct_a & !correct_b)), 2))$p.value))
}

# The detectability floor: the lowest severity stratum whose skill clears the
# pre-registered threshold. Strata must be supplied in ascending order.
detectability_floor <- function(stratum, skill, threshold = 0.50) {
  ok <- which(!is.na(skill) & skill >= threshold)
  if (!length(ok)) return(NA_character_)
  as.character(stratum[min(ok)])
}

# The three confirmatory tests form one family; Holm controls it.
holm_family <- function(p, labels) {
  data.frame(test = labels, p_raw = p,
             p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"), row.names = NULL)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: eval-checks-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
chk <- function(what, expected, got, tol = 1e-8)
  data.frame(check = what, expected = round(expected, 4),
             got = round(got, 4), passes = abs(expected - got) < tol)

# Perfectly separable scores: the 0.90-precision threshold recovers every
# positive, so recall is exactly 1.
s1 <- 10:1; p1 <- c(rep(TRUE, 5), rep(FALSE, 5))
r1 <- recall_at_threshold(s1, p1, threshold_at_precision(s1, p1, 0.90))

# Inverted scores: precision peaks at 0.5, never reaches 0.90, so the operating
# point does not exist and recall must be 0 rather than an accidental number.
p2 <- c(rep(FALSE, 5), rep(TRUE, 5))
r2 <- recall_at_threshold(s1, p2, threshold_at_precision(s1, p2, 0.90))

# A constant offset of 1: RMSE and MAE are 1, and relative RMSE is 1 / mean(obs).
o3 <- c(1, 2, 3); p3 <- o3 + 1

# Theil proportions sum to one for any non-degenerate pair, and U is 0 when
# prediction is exact.
t4 <- theil(c(0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.8), c(0.2, 0.3, 0.25, 0.9))
t5 <- theil(o3, o3)

# Pure bias: prediction is observation plus a constant, so all of the mean
# squared error is the bias term and none of it is variance or covariance.
t6 <- theil(o3, p3)

# Eight positive fold differences: the one-sided signed-rank p is 2^-8.
d7 <- seq(0.1, 0.8, by = 0.1)
w7 <- paired_fold_test(d7)

# Holm is never anti-conservative.
h8 <- holm_family(c(0.01, 0.02, 0.03), c("H1", "H2", "H3"))

# Skill clears 0.50 first in the third stratum.
f9 <- detectability_floor(c("0.01", "0.03", "0.05", "0.10"),
                          c(0.10, 0.20, 0.55, 0.70))

# A confusion matrix with one known error: class a is predicted for one true b,
# so user's accuracy for a is 2/3 and producer's accuracy for b is 1/2.
c10 <- confusion(c("a", "a", "b", "b"), c("a", "a", "a", "b"))

checks <- rbind(
  chk("recall at 0.90 precision, separable", 1, r1),
  chk("recall when 0.90 precision unreachable", 0, r2),
  chk("RMSE of a unit offset", 1, rmse(o3, p3)),
  chk("MAE of a unit offset", 1, mae(o3, p3)),
  chk("relative RMSE, mean 2", 0.5, rrmse(o3, p3)),
  chk("Theil proportions sum to one", 1, sum(t4[c("bias", "variance",
                                                  "covariance")])),
  chk("Theil U of an exact prediction", 0, t5[["U"]]),
  chk("pure offset is all bias", 1, t6[["bias"]]),
  chk("pure offset has no variance term", 0, t6[["variance"]]),
  chk("one-sided Wilcoxon on 8 positives", 2^-8, w7[["p_value"]], 1e-6),
  chk("bootstrap interval brackets the mean", 1,
      as.numeric(w7[["ci_low"]] <= mean(d7) && w7[["ci_high"]] >= mean(d7))),
  chk("Holm is not anti-conservative", 1,
      as.numeric(all(h8$p_holm >= h8$p_raw))),
  chk("detectability floor is the lowest clearing stratum", 0.05,
      as.numeric(f9)),
  chk("user's accuracy for class a", 2 / 3, c10$users[c10$class == "a"]),
  chk("producer's accuracy for class b", 0.5,
      c10$producers[c10$class == "b"]))

stopifnot(all(checks$passes))
```

All `r nrow(checks)` checks listed in Table S9 pass, which is the only reason the document renders past this point; two encode decisions rather than arithmetic, that the harness returns zero recall when no threshold reaches the required precision, and that the bootstrap resamples folds rather than cells, so spatial dependence stays inside the resampling unit.

# Results

Values in this section populate when the pre-registered analysis executes; every table below is rendered from the analysis code with its final structure, and cells display as pending until model training completes. No value in this section is estimated, assumed or illustrative. The section is written in the present tense throughout, unlike the completed Methods sections, because the analyses it reports have not run and describing them in the past would assert work that has not happened. Each subsection states the decision rule its table will be read against, all of them fixed by pre-registration, so the reading is committed before the numbers arrive rather than fitted to them.

## Severity skill

@tbl-severity reports severity-estimation skill per severity stratum for the two deep learning models and the SWIR change baseline on identical stand cells, read down the strata rather than across the models, because the question is where skill fails rather than which model wins, and giving root-mean-square error, relative RMSE normalised by the stratum mean of the reference severity, mean absolute error, and Theil's U with its bias, variance and covariance proportions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-severity
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Severity estimation error per severity stratum and model, from block spatial cross-validation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
strata_lab <- c("0-0.01", "0.01-0.03", "0.03-0.05", "0.05-0.10",
                "0.10-0.20", ">0.20")
models <- c("TempCNN", "Transformer", "SWIR baseline")
sev_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
sev_shell[c("RMSE", "rRMSE", "MAE", "U_Theil", "U_bias", "U_var", "U_cov")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(sev_shell, right = c("RMSE","rRMSE","MAE","U_Theil","U_bias","U_var","U_cov"))
```

## Detection skill

@tbl-detection reports the confusion-matrix summary per stratum, user's and producer's accuracy and the primary metric, recall at 0.90 precision, with fold-wise dispersion. The detectability floor of each method is read from this table as the lowest stratum whose recall at 0.90 precision reaches 0.50, a rule and a threshold both fixed before any outcome was seen, so the floor is located rather than chosen. Table S10 carries the H1 test, the fold-wise paired difference in the primary metric between each deep model and the baseline within the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, its block-bootstrap confidence interval, the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic, and the McNemar cell-level check. The detectability floor of each model is the lowest stratum whose primary metric exceeds the pre-registered threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detection
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Detection skill per severity stratum and model, giving user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and recall at 0.90 precision (R90, the pre-registered primary metric), with fold-wise standard deviation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
det_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
det_shell[c("UA", "PA", "R90", "R90_sd")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(det_shell, right = c("UA","PA","R90","R90_sd"))
```

## Onset dating

@tbl-onset reports onset-year error under the two supervision regimes, testing H2, and gives mean absolute error and root-mean-square error in years, the share of predictions falling within the label bracket, and the fold-wise paired difference between triangulated and single-epoch supervision. The share falling inside the bracket is the more informative column, because mean absolute error against a bracketed truth penalises a prediction that is correct in every sense the labels can express.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-onset
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Onset-year estimation error by model and supervision regime (triangulated two-epoch intervals against single-epoch labels), with the H2 paired test. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
onset_shell <- expand.grid(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                           Supervision = c("Triangulated", "Single-epoch"),
                           KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
onset_shell[c("MAE_yr", "RMSE_yr", "In_bracket", "Delta_MAE", "Wilcoxon_p")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(onset_shell, right = c("MAE_yr","RMSE_yr","In_bracket","Delta_MAE","Wilcoxon_p"))
```

## Climate contribution

@tbl-climate reports H3 as fold-wise paired differences in the primary detection metric and in onset error between climate-augmented and spectral-only models. The pairing is what carries the test, since the two arms differ in their input channels alone and are trained on identical folds, so a difference cannot be attributed to the split. All three confirmatory tests belong to one family and are corrected together by the Holm procedure, which means each is read at its corrected level rather than at 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-climate
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Test of H3, climate-augmented against spectral-only models, fold-wise paired differences with Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
h3_shell <- data.frame(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                       Delta_R90 = "pending", Delta_MAE_yr = "pending",
                       CI95 = "pending", Wilcoxon_p = "pending")
fmt_tbl(h3_shell, right = c("Delta_R90", "Delta_MAE_yr", "CI95", "Wilcoxon_p"))
```
